coverage_gaps: Need a later layer to build a company universe across U.S., Taiwan, Japan, Korea, Europe, and potentially A-share/H-share suppliers instead of only U.S. mega-cap seeds.
Need current valuation and market-pricing checks, but this Layer 1A intentionally avoids buy/sell recommendations, target prices, or return forecasts.
Need primary-source validation for HBM suppliers, optical-module suppliers, substrate/interposer vendors, and advanced packaging equipment vendors beyond the pilot universe.
Need to distinguish demand aggregators from bottleneck owners: hyperscalers may drive demand but may not capture the highest incremental margin if scarce suppliers have stronger bargaining power.
Need falsification tests for each node: capex cuts, AI workload efficiency improvements, oversupply, customer insourcing, export controls, regulatory delays, grid bottlenecks, and commoditization.
Need region-specific regulation review for export controls, nuclear licensing, grid permitting, cybersecurity procurement, and data-sovereignty requirements.

memory_update.text: Technology should be decomposed as an AI infrastructure stack linking software demand, cloud deployment, semiconductors, networking, cybersecurity, and physical power/cooling/grid constraints.
AI accelerator exposure should be analyzed together with HBM, foundry, advanced packaging, substrates, and test capacity because the bottleneck can migrate across these layers.
Data-center power and cooling are first-order technology supply-chain nodes, not merely utilities exposure, because AI deployment can be constrained by time-to-power and thermal capacity.
AI networking and optical interconnect deserve separate coverage from compute accelerators because cluster economics depend on utilization, latency, bandwidth, and congestion control.

Cybersecurity and software supply-chain assurance should be treated as an enabling constraint for cloud and AI adoption, especially where procurement, SBOM, identity, and secure-by-design requirements matter.
Next layers should add non-U.S. public suppliers in Taiwan, Japan, Korea, Europe, and China to avoid a pilot-universe bias toward U.S. mega-cap demand aggregators.

summary: Layer 1A decomposes Technology into six researchable chokepoint lanes rather than a single mega-cap software or semiconductor story: AI compute accelerators plus HBM and advanced packaging; semiconductor equipment and process capacity; AI networking and optical interconnect; cloud AI platforms and automation software; cybersecurity and software supply-chain assurance; and data-center power, cooling, and grid infrastructure. The highest-quality funnel should first map where demand is real and measurable, then test whether value accrues to scarce physical capacity, qualification-heavy components, or software/control layers with high switching costs. This is research support only and does not provide buy/sell recommendations.

theme_map.public_market_search_strategy: Build the universe by supply-chain role, not by popularity. Start with public companies and funds exposed to each node, then classify them as demand aggregators, scarce capacity owners, equipment enablers, high-switching-cost software platforms, regulated infrastructure providers, or theme-adjacent names. For each candidate, require at least one hard evidence path: filing disclosure, segment revenue change, customer concentration or design-win evidence, capacity expansion, backlog/order commentary, regulatory approval, certification, or capex-linked demand signal. Avoid making the funnel a single-ticker exercise; compare each public asset against substitutes and against the bottleneck it claims to control.
supply_side_constraints: Advanced-node foundry capacity, CoWoS/2.5D/3D packaging capacity, HBM supply, substrates, and high-end test capacity
Long lead-time semiconductor equipment, especially lithography, deposition, etch, inspection, advanced packaging, and test tools
High-speed Ethernet/InfiniBand/optical interconnect, DSPs, switch ASICs, NICs, retimers, coherent optics, lasers, connectors, and thermal limits inside AI clusters
Power availability, grid interconnection queues, transformers, switchgear, UPS systems, liquid cooling, backup generation, and water constraints for large data centers
Enterprise adoption friction for AI software: data quality, integration complexity, governance, security, cost management, and measurable ROI
Cybersecurity labor shortage, vulnerability remediation backlogs, regulatory compliance, third-party software dependency risk, and customer certification cycles
